anchor.surface_text: 7.  The applicant Muhyettin Osmanoğlu was born in 1942 and lives in Diyarbakır. He is the father of Atilla Osmanoğlu, who was born in 1968. Atilla was allegedly detained by the police on 25 March 1996 and subsequently disappeared.

facts.text: At approximately 11 a.m. on 25 March 1996 the applicant saw two men escorting Atilla out of the shop. One man was blonde, tall, beardless with an American-style haircut; the second was thickset, average height, dark skin. Both were armed and carried walkie-talkies.

anchor.surface_text: 11.  At approximately 11 a.m. on 25 March 1996 the applicant arrived at the shop and saw two men escorting Atilla out of the shop. One of the men was blonde, tall and beardless with an “American-style haircut”. The second man was thickset, of average height and with dark skin. The men were armed and carried walkie‑talkies.

facts.text: The two men told the applicant they were police officers taking Atilla to police headquarters to submit a bid for a canteen contract. They took a box of sugar and a kilo of tea. Atilla confirmed they would return in about half an hour, so the applicant did not intervene.

anchor.surface_text: 12.  The two men told the applicant that they were police officers and that they were taking his son to police headquarters so that he could submit a bid for a contract to provide canteen services at police headquarters. The men also took with them a box of sugar and a kilo of tea. When the two men told the applicant that they would return Atilla in about half an hour and Atilla confirmed this, the applicant decided not to intervene.

facts.text: Applicant saw Atilla being led to a car with two other occupants. Neighbouring shop owners also witnessed the two men taking Atilla with them.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant saw Atilla being led to a car that contained two other occupants. Neighbouring shop owners also witnessed the two men taking Atilla with them.

facts.text: The same two men had previously visited the shop, claiming to come from the canteen, and asked Atilla to go with them. Atilla refused; the men sat in the shop for about an hour making three coded phone calls. Atilla was worried about this incident.

anchor.surface_text: 13.  The same two men had previously visited the shop, stating that they had come from the canteen, and had asked Atilla to go with them. When Atilla had refused to go, the two men had sat in the shop for about an hour and had made three telephone calls, which Atilla said he did not understand as the men had spoken in code. Atilla had been worried about the incident when he had related it to the applicant that evening.

facts.text: When Atilla did not return on the evening of 25 March 1996, the applicant thought he had been detained. The applicant applied to the governor's office and the chief prosecutor's office at the State Security Court on 26 March and repeatedly thereafter.

anchor.surface_text: 14.  When Atilla did not return on the evening of 25 March 1996, the applicant thought that he had been detained in custody. The following day he applied to the governor's office and also to the chief prosecutor's office at the State Security Court. He applied again to the same prosecutor on 29 March and on 1, 9 and 19 April. On 16 May 1996 the applicant applied once again to the governor's office.

facts.text: On 1 April 1996 the prosecutor replied that Atilla's name did not feature in custody records.

anchor.surface_text: 15.  The applicant received a reply to his petition of 1 April 1996 from the prosecutor at the State Security Court, who stated that his son's name did not feature in the custody records.

facts.text: In June 1996 the applicant was summoned before the Diyarbakır State Security Court regarding his petitions. He was told to contact the murder desk at Diyarbakır police headquarters, to which he applied but received no substantive response.

anchor.surface_text: 16.  In June 1996 the applicant was summoned before the Diyarbakır State Security Court in connection with his petitions. The statement and the complaint he made were filed under preliminary file number 1996/4041. In relation to his petition to the governor's office, the applicant was told to contact the murder desk at Diyarbakır police headquarters. The applicant applied by letter to that authority but did not receive a response other than a request to identify a number of unidentified bodies found in the area.

facts.text: On 20 May 1996 a statement was taken from the applicant at the murder desk of Diyarbakır police headquarters. Atilla Osmanoğlu was registered as a missing person and an investigation was carried out throughout the country to find him.

facts.text: The applicant is a retired civil servant who moved from Hazro to Diyarbakır in February 1992 after an officer threatened his son. In 1994 the applicant was detained for 28 days and ill-treated but later acquitted.

anchor.surface_text: 10. The applicant is a retired civil servant. At the time of the events giving rise to the present application he and his family lived in Diyarbakır, where his son Atilla ran the wholesale grocery shop owned by the applicant. Prior to living in Diyarbakır the applicant and his family had lived in the nearby town of Hazro, where he worked as a civil servant. In February 1992 the applicant and his family moved to Diyarbakır after an officer threatened his son. In 1994 the applicant was detained for 28 days and was subjected to ill-treatment during his detention. He was subsequently acquitted of the charges against him.

facts.text: The applicant gave a description of the two men who took his son and stated he could identify them if he saw them again. He also said the neighbouring shop owner witnessed the abduction and could be questioned.

anchor.surface_text: 26.  A statement was taken from the applicant on 20 May 1996 at the murder desk of Diyarbakır police headquarters. The applicant reiterated the content of his previous statements and gave a description of the two men who had taken his son away. He stated that he would be able to identify the two men if he saw them again. He also added that the same two men had visited his shop two days before they had taken his son, and that after leaving his shop they had gone to a neighbouring shop. The applicant pointed out that the owner of the neighbouring shop could be questioned in order to establish the identity of the police officers.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that his son had been taken into the custody of the police and had subsequently disappeared in circumstances engaging the responsibility of the respondent State under Articles 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 and 14 of the Convention.

concepts.interpretation: Article 2 enshrines the right to life and imposes both negative and positive obligations on the State, including the duty to protect life and to conduct effective investigations into deaths or disappearances.

anchor.surface_text: Relying on Article 5 of the Convention, the applicant alleged that his son had been the victim of a violation of that provision on account of his arbitrary and unacknowledged detention by State authorities and/or the failure and/or refusal of the State to conduct a prompt and effective investigation into his complaints.

concepts.interpretation: Article 5 protects liberty and security; the Court found no violation on the basis of lack of evidence of detention by State agents but noted investigation failures.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant submitted that the prolonged distress and anguish caused by his son's disappearance over the past eleven years amounted to a violation of his right to respect for family life within the meaning of Article 8 of the Convention.

concepts.interpretation: Article 8 protects family life; the Court found no need to examine separately given findings under Articles 2 and 3.

anchor.surface_text: Relying on Article 13 of the Convention, the applicant submitted that he had been denied an effective remedy in respect of his Convention complaints.

concepts.interpretation: Article 13 requires effective remedies; the Court found violation of Article 2 procedural limb sufficed and did not examine separately.

anchor.surface_text: the authorities' failure to initiate a prompt and effective investigation into the disappearance of his son had directly endangered his son's life and constituted a violation of the State's positive obligation to protect life pursuant to Article 2 of the Convention.

concepts.interpretation: The State has a positive obligation under Article 2 to take operational measures to protect life when there is a real and immediate risk, including conducting effective investigations into disappearances.

anchor.surface_text: the scope of the positive obligation must be interpreted in a way which does not impose an impossible or disproportionate burden on the authorities.

concepts.interpretation: The positive obligation to protect life is limited by proportionality and reasonableness, not requiring impossible or disproportionate measures.

anchor.surface_text: For a positive obligation to arise, it must be established that the authorities knew or ought to have known at the time of the existence of a real and immediate risk to the life of an identified individual or individuals from the criminal acts of a third party and that they failed to take measures within the scope of their powers which, judged reasonably, might have been expected to avoid that risk (see Osman, cited above, § 116).

concepts.interpretation: The Osman test requires knowledge or constructive knowledge of a real and immediate risk to life and failure to take reasonable measures to prevent it for a positive obligation under Article 2 to arise.

anchor.surface_text: Relying on Article 13 of the Convention, the applicant submitted that he had been denied an effective remedy in respect of his Convention complaints.

concepts.interpretation: The Court considered the lack of effective investigation under Article 2 procedural limb also relevant to Article 13's requirement for effective remedies.

anchor.surface_text: the scope of the positive obligation must be interpreted in a way which does not impose an impossible or disproportionate burden on the authorities.

concepts.interpretation: The margin of appreciation doctrine allows States discretion in how they fulfill positive obligations, balancing operational realities and rights protection.

anchor.surface_text: The Court has generally applied the standard of proof “beyond reasonable doubt” (see Ireland v. the United Kingdom, judgment of 18 January 1978, Series A no. 25, § 161).

concepts.interpretation: The Court applies an autonomous standard of proof 'beyond reasonable doubt' in establishing facts, especially in cases involving serious allegations such as disappearances and deaths.

1.  Holds unanimously that there has been no violation of Article 2 of the Convention in respect of the abduction of the applicant's son, allegedly by agents of the State, and his subsequent presumed death;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court was unable to establish definitively State agent responsibility for the abduction and disappearance of the applicant's son due to lack of evidence and investigation.
